title: Cycling: Pedal Power
summary: How the bicycle developed, how pedals, chains, and gears make it move, why cycling is healthy and efficient, and how riders race and stay safe.
poll: Riding a bike is better than riding in a car for short trips.

versions.title: Pedal Power
versions.text:
Do you like to ride a bike? It is fun. It is good for you, too.

The first bike was made in 1817. It had no pedals! The rider sat on it. He ran with his feet to push it.

Then bikes got pedals on the front wheel. Some had a huge front wheel. They were hard to ride.

Next came a new bike. Its wheels were the same size. It had a chain. This bike was safe.

You push the pedals. The pedals turn the chain. The chain turns the back wheel.

Some bikes have gears. A low gear makes it easy to go up a hill. A high gear helps you go fast on flat ground.

It is hard to balance on a bike that stands still. Once it moves, it is not so hard. You steer to stay up.

A bike needs no gas. It does not make the air dirty. Riding makes your heart and legs strong.

Some people race bikes. One big race in France lasts three weeks!

In Saudi Arabia, it is hot. Ride in the cool morning. Drink lots of water. Wear a helmet. It keeps your head safe.

In the 1880s, a new kind of bike changed everything. Its two wheels were the same size, and a chain turned the back wheel. This bike was much safer. Bikes today still look like it. Soon, tires filled with air made rides softer, too.

Here is how a bike works. When you push the pedals, they turn a chain. The chain turns the back wheel, and the bike rolls forward.

Many bikes have gears. A low gear makes pedaling easy when you climb a hill. A high gear helps you go fast on flat ground.

It is hard to balance on a bike that is standing still. Once the bike is moving, it is easier. You make small turns to stay up.

versions.title: Cycling: Pedal Power
versions.text:
Around the world, people ride bicycles for fun, for exercise, and to get from place to place. Cycling is also an exciting sport with races that last for weeks.

The first bicycle was built in 1817 in Germany. It had no pedals at all. The rider sat on a seat and pushed against the ground with his feet, almost like running while sitting down.

In the 1860s, inventors added pedals to the front wheel. Later, some bikes had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, because a bigger wheel traveled farther with each turn of the pedals. These bikes were fast but tall and unsteady, and falls were common.

In the 1880s, a new design called the safety bicycle changed everything. Its two wheels were the same size, and a chain carried power to the back wheel. Most bikes today still follow this shape. Soon after, inventors added tires filled with air, which made the ride far more comfortable.

When you push the pedals, they turn a toothed wheel that pulls the chain. The chain turns the back wheel, and the bike rolls forward.

Many bikes have gears. A low gear makes pedaling easier when you climb a hill, though you move more slowly. A high gear is harder to push, but it lets you go faster on flat ground.

Balancing on a bike that is standing still is very hard. Once the bike is moving, it becomes easier, because the rider can make small steering changes to stay upright.

Cycling is one of the most efficient ways to travel. A bike needs no fuel and does not pollute the air. Riding regularly strengthens the heart, lungs, and leg muscles, and it is gentle on the knees.

Bike racing tests endurance. The Tour de France, which began in 1903, covers about 3,500 kilometers in three weeks.

In Saudi Arabia, professional races are held in the desert near AlUla. Riders there go in the cool morning or evening, drink plenty of water, and always wear helmets.

versions.title: Pedal Power: The Science and Sport of Cycling
versions.text:
Around the entire world, people routinely ride bicycles for recreation, for physical exercise, and simply to travel efficiently from one place to another, and competitive cycling also constitutes a thrilling professional sport featuring certain grueling competitions that continue uninterrupted for multiple consecutive weeks.

The very first bicycle, originally constructed in 1817 within Germany, possessed no pedals whatsoever. The seated rider instead propelled the entire machine by rhythmically pushing against the ground with his own feet, functioning almost like running while remaining seated throughout.

During the 1860s, inventive engineers attached pedals to the front wheel assembly, and later certain bicycles featured an enormous front wheel paired with a tiny rear wheel, because a proportionally larger wheel traveled farther with each individual rotation of the pedals, although these particular machines proved tall and inherently unstable, and consequently dangerous falls occurred with troubling frequency.

During the 1880s, a fully new design officially called the safety bicycle transformed cycling as a practice, since its two wheels were manufactured identical in size and a connecting chain efficiently transferred power to the rear wheel, a fundamental mechanical arrangement that the large majority of bicycles still faithfully follow today. Soon afterward, inventors introduced pneumatic tires. These are filled internally with pressurized air. These innovative tires made the overall riding experience more comfortable.

When a rider pushes down forcefully on the pedals, this motion rotates a toothed gear wheel that later pulls the connecting chain. This in turn rotates the rear wheel and thereby propels the entire bicycle forward with mechanical efficiency.

Many modern bicycles feature several distinct gears: a conveniently low gear makes pedaling easier when climbing a steep hill, although you consequently move more slowly overall. Meanwhile, a correspondingly high gear requires greatly greater physical effort but permits you to travel faster across level ground.

Balancing upon a stationary bicycle proves extraordinarily difficult in practice. Once the bicycle begins moving, however, balancing becomes easier to maintain. This happened because the rider can make small, instinctive steering adjustments in order to remain upright and stable.

Cycling constitutes one of the most efficient methods of human transportation available, since a bicycle requires no fuel whatsoever and generates no atmospheric pollution during operation, and riding regularly greatly strengthens the heart, lungs, and leg muscles, while placing relatively minimal cumulative strain upon the body's joints.

Professional competitive racing demands truly tremendous physical endurance. The legendary Tour de France, which originally began in 1903, covers approximately 3,500 kilometers across three grueling weeks, and competing racers crouch low and wear specialized smooth clothing to become more aerodynamic, and they also frequently ride together in tightly organized formations, because cyclists positioned behind the leading rider encounter greatly less air resistance and consequently conserve valuable physical energy.

Within Saudi Arabia, professional cycling races are regularly held throughout the desert region near AlUla. There, competing athletes train during the cooler morning or evening hours, consume plentiful water, and wear protective helmets at all times.

versions.title: Pedal Power: The Science and Sport of Cycling

Around the entire inhabited world, people routinely ride bicycles for leisurely recreation, for structured physical exercise, and simply to travel efficiently from one location to another, and competitive cycling additionally constitutes a thrilling professional spectator sport featuring certain grueling, multi-stage competitions that continue uninterrupted for multiple consecutive weeks at considerable physical cost to participants.

The very first documented bicycle, originally constructed in 1817 within Germany, possessed absolutely no pedals whatsoever as a mechanical feature; the seated rider instead propelled the entire wooden machine by rhythmically pushing against the ground directly with his own feet, functioning almost precisely like running while nevertheless remaining seated throughout the entire exercise.

During the 1860s, inventive mechanical engineers attached pedals directly to the front wheel assembly for the first time, and subsequently certain bicycle designs featured an enormous front wheel paired incongruously with a comparatively tiny rear wheel, because a proportionally larger wheel traveled considerably farther with each individual rotation of the pedals, although these particular machines proved genuinely tall, precarious, and inherently unstable in practice, and consequently dangerous falls occurred with troubling, well-documented frequency among riders.

During the 1880s, an entirely new engineering design formally called the safety bicycle fundamentally and permanently transformed cycling as a widespread practice, since its two wheels were manufactured to be identical in size and a connecting mechanical chain efficiently transferred power directly to the rear wheel, a fundamental mechanical arrangement that the overwhelming majority of bicycles still faithfully follow even today. Soon afterward, inventive engineers successfully introduced pneumatic tires, which are filled internally with carefully pressurized air, and these innovative tires made the overall riding experience considerably more comfortable and less physically jarring.

When a rider pushes down forcefully and rhythmically on the pedals, this repeated motion rotates a toothed gear wheel that subsequently pulls the connecting mechanical chain, which in turn rotates the rear wheel and thereby propels the entire bicycle forward with considerable mechanical efficiency.

Many modern bicycles feature several distinct, selectable gears: a conveniently low gear makes pedaling considerably easier when ascending a steep hill, although you consequently move more slowly overall as a direct result, while a correspondingly high gear requires substantially greater physical effort from the rider but permits considerably faster travel across level, unobstructed ground.

Balancing successfully upon an entirely stationary bicycle proves extraordinarily, almost counterintuitively difficult in actual practice; once the bicycle begins moving forward, however, balancing becomes considerably easier to maintain reliably, because the rider can continuously make small, largely instinctive steering adjustments in order to remain upright and dynamically stable while in motion.

Cycling constitutes, by most measures, one of the most genuinely efficient methods of human transportation currently available, since a bicycle requires absolutely no fuel input whatsoever and generates no atmospheric pollution whatsoever during ordinary operation, and riding regularly substantially strengthens the heart, lungs, and leg muscles over time, while placing relatively minimal cumulative strain upon the body's weight-bearing joints.

Professional competitive racing demands truly tremendous and sustained physical endurance from its participants. The legendary Tour de France, which originally began in 1903, covers approximately 3,500 grueling kilometers across three demanding weeks, and competing racers crouch remarkably low over their handlebars and wear specialized smooth, form-fitting clothing specifically engineered to become considerably more aerodynamic, and they additionally frequently ride together in tightly organized pack formations, because cyclists positioned directly behind the leading rider encounter substantially reduced air resistance and consequently conserve genuinely valuable physical energy reserves for later stages.

Within Saudi Arabia, professional cycling races are regularly held throughout the desert region surrounding AlUla, where competing athletes deliberately train during the considerably cooler morning or evening hours, consume plentiful water continuously throughout, and consistently wear protective helmets at all times without exception.

MID.prompt: Explain how changes to the bicycle's design made riding safer and easier. Use at least three details from the article.
checklist: I described at least two changes in bicycle design.
I explained how each change helped riders.
I used at least three details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Early bicycles had no pedals at all, so riders pushed against the ground with their feet, which made riding slow and tiring. Later, inventors added pedals and a chain, and the safety bicycle design made both wheels the same size instead of one giant front wheel, which made the ride much more stable than the tall, unsteady early bikes. Adding air-filled tires and multiple gears, which make pedaling easier on hills or faster on flat ground, made cycling both safer and more comfortable.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how science helps cyclists, from the design of the bicycle to the way professional racers ride. Use at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained at least one way bicycle design uses science.
I explained at least one way racers use science to save energy.
I supported my explanation with three pieces of evidence.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Science helps cyclists in many ways, starting with the bicycle's design. The chain-driven safety bicycle, with two equal-sized wheels, is far more stable and efficient than the old high-wheeled bikes, and air-filled, or pneumatic, tires make the ride smoother by absorbing bumps. Gears also use science, letting a rider choose a low gear that makes climbing hills easier or a high gear that lets them ride faster on flat ground. Professional racers in events like the Tour de France or the desert races near AlUla also rely on aerodynamic positions and careful training to build endurance over thousands of kilometers, showing that science shapes cycling from the machine itself to the rider's body.
